meta.title: Who really said "Written Without Fear and Without Research"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker. The historian Carl L. Becker wrote it in 1912, about a book on socialism — and the page is still legible in the scanned volume.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Written Without Fear and Without Research'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is thirty-two years older than the Parker attribution. Carl L. Becker aimed it at A. M. Simons in a paper read to the American Historical Association.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — actually Carl L. Becker
answer.authorDates: 1873–1945 · American historian, professor at the University of Kansas and later Cornell
answer.sourceLine: Becker used the phrase in “The Reviewing of Historical Books,” printed in the Annual Report of the American Historical Association for the Year 1912 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1914), p. 133. He was dismissing A. M. Simons’s Social Forces in American History: “not perhaps a very wise performance; written, it must be confessed, without fear and without research.” The line reached Dorothy Parker only in 1944, in an anthology, with no book and no review attached.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Annual Report of the American Historical Association for the Year 1912 (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1914), pp. 127–140
Carl Becker, then Professor of History at the University of Kansas
Social Forces in American History by A. M. Simons

source.excerpt: The great books, however, are not the only ones that enlist the attention of the critical reviewer. It sometimes happens that a slight book is significant for what it points to. I have in mind, for example, the little volume of Mr. A. M. Simons, entitled “Social Forces in American History”; not perhaps a very wise performance; written, it must be confessed, without fear and without research; written nevertheless with profound conviction, and significant because it is representative of what probably passes for history among militant socialists…
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “historian Carl L. Becker used this expression by 1912, and currently he is the strongest candidate for originator known to QI,” adding that “Dorothy Parker may have used the expression, but the evidence is indirect, and the linkage appeared many years after the phrase was already being disseminated.”

We did not stop at the anchor. The 1914 volume is scanned in full at the Internet Archive ↗, and the sentence is there on page 133, in the paper “The Reviewing of Historical Books” by Carl Becker — word for word as Quote Investigator reports it.

It spread as a borrowed quip among historians long before Parker was named: Quote Investigator records it in quotation marks and without attribution in Thomas Reed Powell’s New Republic piece of 7 February 1923, in S. E. Morison in The New England Quarterly in January 1928, and in Charles A. Beard in 1940. Marks around a phrase are how a writer signals it is not theirs.

The Parker credit enters in 1944, in Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me: “She polished off one scientific volume with the dictum, ‘It was written without fear and without research.’” Quote Investigator ↗ notes that no book title and no review is given — and none has been produced since.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned volume at the Internet Archive, page 133. Obvious scanning artefacts in the optical character recognition have been silently corrected; the wording is otherwise as printed.

author.name: Carl L. Becker
author.heading: About Carl L. Becker
author.metaLine: 1873–1945 · American historian; Professor of History at the University of Kansas 1902–1916, then at Cornell 1917–1941
author.bio: Carl Lotus Becker was one of the most stylish American historians of his generation, and the phrase that escaped him is a fair sample of the prose. He taught at the University of Kansas for fourteen years before moving to Cornell, where he spent the rest of his career. His best-known book, The Heavenly City of the Eighteenth-Century Philosophers (1932), is still read — and it is where he used the same phrase a second time, about words “permitted to slip off the tongue or the pen without fear and without research.”

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Parker is the name the line travels under, and she is the last person in its documented history, not the first. The chain of credits is worth laying out because each link is dated.

items.why: The earliest link to Parker is Bennett Cerf’s anthology Try and Stop Me in 1944 — thirty-two years after Becker’s printed use — and it names no book, no magazine and no date, per Quote Investigator ↗. Robert E. Drennan’s The Algonquin Wits repeated the credit in 1968 and called it a book review.

Drennan is the source for several Parker attributions that have since collapsed. Wikiquote ↗ lists “You can’t teach an old dogma new tricks” as attributed to Parker by Drennan and then found anonymously fifteen years earlier, and notes that for “This is not a novel to be tossed aside lightly” Drennan’s source “seems to be a Parker review which does not seem to contain this quote.”

Becker aimed it at A. M. Simons’s Social Forces in American History in a paper printed in the Annual Report of the American Historical Association for the Year 1912 ↗, p. 133. He used the phrase again in The Heavenly City of the Eighteenth Century Philosophers in 1932.

items.scope: The other book it is pinned to
items.why: Becker did apply the phrase to Carnegie as well — Clifton Fadiman quoted him doing so in The New Yorker of 5 April 1941: “Dr. Becker refers neatly to that eminent library-lover’s naive volume, ‘Triumphant Democracy,’ as ‘written without fear and without research.’” That is a second Becker target, not a rival origin, and it is recorded by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The phrase is Carl L. Becker’s, from 1912, and the page is scanned and readable. Parker’s name was attached to it in 1944 by an anthologist who cited nothing.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Becker was not being merely rude. His paper was an argument that American historians reviewed books badly — politely, vaguely, and without the nerve to say what a book was worth — and the Simons demolition was his demonstration of the alternative.

The joke has a hinge in it. “Without fear” is praise; “without research” turns the compliment inside out in three words. That structure is exactly why it detached from its author and floated free among reviewers for thirty years before anyone thought to ask whose it was.
detailsBody: Read in full, Becker’s verdict on Simons is more generous than the fragment suggests. He goes on to call the book “written nevertheless with profound conviction, and significant because it is representative of what probably passes for history among militant socialists” — and predicts that in the next fifty years many better histories of the United States would be written from the same point of view. He was right about that.

Why the line drifted to Parker is no mystery. She was the period’s designated wit, and an unclaimed quip about a bad book had an obvious home. Wikiquote’s Parker page carries a standing warning about exactly this habit, asking readers to verify the provenance of anything ascribed to her.
context.pull: “Without fear” is a compliment until the next three words arrive.

sourcesVerified.claim: Carl Becker’s paper "The Reviewing of Historical Books" appears in the Annual Report of the American Historical Association for the Year 1912, beginning at page 127, and the phrase "written, it must be confessed, without fear and without research" is on page 133, aimed at A. M. Simons’s Social Forces in American History.
Quote Investigator concludes Carl L. Becker used the expression by 1912 and is the strongest known candidate for originator, and that the Parker linkage appeared many years later and is indirect.
Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me (1944) is the earliest link to Parker and reads "She polished off one scientific volume with the dictum, ‘It was written without fear and without research.’"
The phrase appears in quotation marks and unattributed in Thomas Reed Powell (New Republic, 7 Feb 1923), S. E. Morison (New England Quarterly, Jan 1928) and Charles A. Beard (1940).
Clifton Fadiman, The New Yorker, 5 April 1941, quotes Becker applying the phrase to Andrew Carnegie’s Triumphant Democracy.

Wikiquote records that Drennan’s The Algonquin Wits (1968) is the source of Parker credits that do not hold up, including "You can’t teach an old dogma new tricks" and "This is not a novel to be tossed aside lightly".
Carl Lotus Becker lived 1873–1945, taught at the University of Kansas from 1902 to 1916 and at Cornell from 1917, and wrote The Heavenly City of the Eighteenth-Century Philosophers (1932).
